Issued at 127 PM EST Sun Nov 22 2026

Warm temperatuers continue to dominate northern lower and eastern 
upper today as gusty south winds are seen ahead of an approaching 
cold front. This warm sector stretches into far east Ontario and 
central Quebec CAN. Water vapor satellite shows a narrow baroclinic 
leaf trekking across the U.P. of MI and Ontario, showcasing the 
stark temperatures differences driving this intensifying system. 
Warm sector rain showers will continue across northern MI into this 
evening. Light to moderate rain will start and end fairly quickly 
for most locations, as a cold front builds in quickly behind. 
Accumulations are expected to remain on the lighter side of a few 
tenths of an inch for most locations due to this shorter duration. 
Winds will shift west to northwest tonight, with gusts of 20 to 25 
mph. In the upper levels, heights will rapidly drop tonight as long 
wave mid to upper troughing builds into the eastern CONUS. A closed 
low (currently over MN) will open up as it reaching Lk Superior 
tonight. Winds will have become mostly northwest by this time as the 
cooler air aloft quickly moves overhead. Although upper level 
temperatures begin to support snow production tonight into 
early Monday morning, cooling at the surface will lag behind. 
The feature that will help bring surface temperatures to 
freezing will be a moisture boundary moving through the state 
from north to south early Monday morning. This will aid in 
shower initiation, as well as turning some rain showers to a 
rain/snow mix if by the coast, or mostly snow shower elsewhere. 
Some lake enhancement will keep isolated showers lingering 
through Monday morning, however any snow accumulation is 
expected to remain well under an inch. 

Temperatures will warm above freezing during the day Monday, 
reaching into the upper 30s to low 40s. A break in shower 
activity is expected during the day as forcing breifly relaxes. 
In the upper levels, a positively tilted short wave will deepen  
Monday afternoon over WI/Lk MI. At the same time, surface high 
pressure will be building into Ontario and the western Great 
Lakes region. Lake aggregate troughing is seen in most high res 
guidance as this surface high pressure attempts to build in 
Monday. As the upper trough deepens and starts to trend towards
a neutral tilt, a vorticity max aloft aligns with this surface 
troughing residing over northern Lk MI. At the same time, the 
cold air aloft has moved overhead (-10C 850 mb temps). Another 
burst of snow showers is expected Monday mid afternoon/evening 
over northwest lower MI as that upper vort max pivots inland. 
Surface temperatures will be in the mid to high 30s for coastal 
areas, however near freezing by then for interior locations. The
instability, combined with the surface forcing and upper level 
vorticity are starting to introduce the potential of a 
mesovortex feature forming. Some high res guidance is hinting at
this potential, and producing fairly high snowfall rates within
this feature. Although the environment theoretically supports 
this, pinning down the exact track and intensity of such a 
feature remains difficult at this time. Also, some CAMs (such as
the HRRR) are bullish with the instability present since there 
is still so much heat in the lakes. After this feature continues
downstate, exiting northern lower by late evening, northwest 
lake effect bands will establish for the remainder of Monday 
night into early Tuesday morning. Overnight snow bands could be 
more loosely defined (clustery) and weaker in nature due to 
weakening low level winds and lowering inversion heights, but 
lingering instability should continue some activity. 

Although uncertainty in exact snow amounts and locations of highest 
snow amounts remains, we can say some things with more certainty. 
Rain will turn to snow Monday morning for interior locations,
with accumulations expected to remain light and anything that 
can accumulate will melt during the day. Another burst of snow 
showers become possible Monday afternoon and evening. The focus
of heaviest snow will be south of Grand Traverse Bay and along
and west of HWY 131, where 1 to 3 inches of snow is expected by
sunrise Tuesday, with locally higher amounts possible. There is
a 30 to 40% chance of locations in Grand Traverse and Kalkaska 
counties could see at least 4 inches of snow total by sunrise 
Tuesday. There is a 15 to 20% chance for locations in Grand 
Traverse County seeing at least 6 inches of snow by sunrise 
Tuesday. These higher amounts will be local in nature, not 
widespread, with most of that falling late Monday afternoon 
through the middle part of Monday night, under heavier snowfall 
rates supported by a possible mesovortex. Due to the possibility
